Starting with Q2: It's selecting pairs of bars (bar1 and bar2) from the Serves table where they serve the same beer, and the bars are different (s1.bar <> s2.bar). So Q2 is essentially finding all pairs of distinct bars that serve at least one common beer. Each row in the result is a pair of bars that share at least one beer.

Now Q1 is more complicated. Let's break it down. The query selects bar1 and bar2 from the Bar table (self-joined). The WHERE clause has two parts connected by AND. 

The first part is NOT EXISTS (SELECT s1.beer FROM serves s1 WHERE s1.bar = b1.name AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM serves s2 WHERE s2.bar = b2.name AND s2.beer = s1.beer)). 

So this part is saying that for bar1 (b1), there does not exist a beer that bar1 serves which bar2 does not serve. In other words, every beer that bar1 serves is also served by bar2. So bar2 serves all beers that bar1 serves. 

The second part is EXISTS (SELECT s2.beer FROM serves s2 WHERE s2.bar = b2.name AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM serves s1 WHERE s1.bar = b1.name AND s1.beer = s2.beer)). 

This part is saying that there exists at least one beer that bar2 serves which bar1 does not serve. So bar2 serves some beer that bar1 doesn't. 

Putting both parts together, Q1 is finding pairs of bars (bar1, bar2) where bar2 serves all the beers that bar1 serves, and also serves at least one beer that bar1 doesn't. So bar2 is a superset of bar1's beers, but not equal. 

So Q1 is looking for bar pairs where bar2 is a strict superset of bar1's beers. 

Comparing that to Q2, which just finds any two bars that share at least one beer. So Q2 is much broader. For example, if two bars both serve beer A, they would be in Q2's result, even if they don't have any other beers in common. But Q1 requires that bar2 has all of bar1's beers plus more. 

Therefore, Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent. 

To create a counterexample, I need a scenario where Q2 returns pairs that Q1 does not. Let's think of a simple case. Suppose there are two bars, Bar A and Bar B. Bar A serves beer X. Bar B serves beer X and Y. 

In this case, Q2 would return (A,B) because they share X. But Q1's conditions: for bar1=A and bar2=B, the first part (NOT EXISTS) checks if all beers of A are served by B. But what if there are two bars, Bar A and Bar B. Bar A serves X and Y. Bar B serves X. Then Q2 would return (A,B) because they share X. But Q1 would not return this pair because the first part (NOT EXISTS) would check if all beers of A (X and Y) are served by B. B only serves X, so the NOT EXISTS part would be false. Hence, the entire WHERE clause would be false. So Q1 would not include (A,B) here. 

But in this case, Q2 includes (A,B) and Q1 does not. So this is a counterexample. 

Another example: suppose Bar A serves X, Bar B serves X. Then Q2 would have (A,B) since they share X. But Q1's first condition requires that all beers of A (X) are served by B (which they are), and the second condition requires that B serves a beer not in A. But B only serves X, which is in A. So the second part would be false. Therefore, Q1 would not return (A,B). 

So in this case, Q2 returns (A,B) but Q1 does not. Hence, the queries are not equivalent. 

So the counterexample would be two bars that serve the same beer, but no other beers. Then Q2 returns them, but Q1 does not.
